content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's core claim is that 'works of the law' has no single fixed referent across its occurrences — sometimes God's own law, sometimes the circumcision-party's demand, sometimes unnamed deeds — while what Paul uniformly denies is the claim made for the deeds: that they can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or put God in debt. This variable-referent, constant-denial reading explains the full spread of cited texts better than either fixed-referent rival. The traditional Reformation reading (works of the law = human effort/legalism generally, with the law itself effectively superseded) cannot comfortably hold Romans 3:31 ('we establish the law'), Romans 7:12-22, Galatians 5:14, 1 Corinthians 7:19, Ephesians 6:2, and Acts 16:3/21:24 alongside the negative statements; the book explains all of these without strain by locating the error in the purchase-claim rather than in the deeds or the law. The New Perspective reading (works of the law = Jewish boundary markers throughout) fits Galatians 2:11-16 and 5:2-6 but breaks on Galatians 3:10, which explicitly quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 about 'all things which are written in the book of the law,' and on Romans 3:20, where the law's function is universal knowledge of sin — texts the book's occurrence-by-occurrence table handles directly. Because the book accommodates both the Antioch/circumcision contexts and the whole-Torah contexts while each rival must explain away one set, and because Romans 4:4-5 and Luke 17:10 supply the debt/wage mechanics the entry names, the book's identification is the best-supported explanation among the actual alternatives. No supplied text is better explained by a counter-reading than by the book's core.","book_core_identification":"'Works of the law' is not a fixed technical code naming one unchanging class of deeds (neither all human moral effort nor Jewish boundary markers only); the surrounding context identifies which deeds are in view (God's law in Rom 3:20, 28 and Gal 3:10; the circumcision-party's demand in Gal 2:16; unnamed acts in Gal 3:2, 5), while the phrase's constant function is to deny a claim made for those deeds — that they can purchase justification, obtain the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt.","book_secondary_elaborations":["'Works of the law' is not a synonym for obedience; a work and obedience can meet in one act without being identical","The wage/debt economics of Romans 4:4-5 and Luke 17:10 as the mechanism of the denied claim","The textual note that Romans 9:32 reads 'works of the law' only in the Received Text behind the KJV","The broader 'end of the law' argument that telos in Romans 10:4 means goal rather than termination","The taxonomy of Paul's named laws (law of God, law of sin, law of faith, law of Christ, commandments of men)","Readings of Colossians 2, Ephesians 2, Hebrews 7-9, Romans 14, and Acts 15 as consistent with the law's continuing definition of right-living"],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, Wright): 'works of the law' is a consistent Second Temple technical phrase (paralleled in 4QMMT) referring primarily to Jewish covenant boundary markers — circumcision, food laws, Sabbath/calendar observance — and Paul's polemic targets ethnic exclusivism and the requirement that Gentiles adopt Jewish identity markers, not human deeds offered as a purchase price generally.","counter_core_identification":"Erga nomou carries one stable referent across all occurrences: the identity badges distinguishing Jews from Gentiles; Paul denies that these badges define covenant membership, and the faith/works antithesis is about who belongs to God's people, not about deeds failing as payment for justification.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that the referent of 'works of the law' varies by context and denies that Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 3:10 have God's law as a whole in view; it insists the phrase uniformly names Jewish boundary practices, so the book's classification of several occurrences as 'God's law — clear' cannot be
